 Gas prices in the US are nearly half of Europe's: Why are American drivers paying so much less?
 SECTIONS Gas prices in the US are nearly half of Europe's: Why are American drivers paying so much less? ET Online Last Updated: Nov 08, 2026, 07:02:00 PM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis American motorists are currently paying much less for fuel compared to drivers in the European Union. The average petrol price in the EU is almost double that of the US, highlighting significant market differences. Higher taxation in Europe contributes to this price discrepancy, making it important for consumers to understand. Diesel costs also reflect a noticeable difference, though the gap is smaller than for petrol.

 TIL Creatives US motorists currently enjoy a significant price advantage over their EU counterparts, particularly when buying petrol. Fuel prices in the United States have become significantly lower compared to prices charged by motorists in the European Union. The disparity is especially evident in petrol prices; in the EU, petrol costs almost twice as much as in the US when expressed in euros per litre.
 According to information provided by the US Energy Information Administration and the European Commission's Weekly Oil Bulletin as of November 2, 2026, the higher price of fuel applies to diesel as well.
Fuel taxes, differences in policies, and oil market structure are among several factors behind the higher price of fuel in Europe. 
 Also Read | Anthropic wants to create new billionaires through its IPO, but American voters are growing tired of Big Tech's wealth explosion 
What is equally significant is that cheap fuel in the US does not mean that oil itself is cheaper in this country. Taxes and other factors determine the cost of fuel.
 Live Events
 How do US gas prices compare with EU petrol prices?
Based on the information presented on November 2, a clear disparity between the two markets can be noted.
 In accordance with the EIA, the average price of US regular gasoline was $4.153 per gallon. With the help of the exchange rate between the euro and dollar of about €1 = $1.1216, it equals about €0.98 per litre.
 Also Read | Hispanic voters helped Trump win in 2024. Now his immigration crackdown could cost him their support 
The European Commission Weekly Oil Bulletin stated the weighted average price of Euro-super 95 gasoline in the EU as €1.929 per litre.
It implies that the average EU price was nearly 97% higher than that of the US.
In other words, European drivers were paying almost double the amount that American consumers paid for the same volume of petrol.
Nevertheless, there are quite significant differences among various member states in terms of petrol prices.
For instance, on November 2, the average petrol price in Malta was €1.340 per litre, whereas in Denmark, it was €2.498 per litre.
 Are US diesel prices also lower than EU diesel prices?
This distinction can also be observed in the diesel market, although the difference between the two is relatively lower compared to the distinction in the petrol market.
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the average US on-highway diesel price on November 2 was $6.292 per gallon. When converted using the same exchange rate, this is approximately €1.48 per litre.
On the other hand, the weighted average for EU diesel, according to the European Commission, was €2.154 per litre during the same week.
The average price of diesel in the EU was approximately 45% higher compared to the American price.
It is significant because diesel is widely used in trucks and in the logistics industry. Increased fuel prices may lead to increased costs for businesses and thus higher prices for consumers.
However, this depends on many other factors, such as fuel efficiency, consumption, transport contracts, and the country where the company operates.
 Why are petrol and diesel prices higher in Europe than in the US?
Taxes are one of the main factors contributing to the disparity in prices for fuel.
In Europe, governments tend to impose hefty excise and value-added taxes on motor fuels. Such taxes account for the final price of fuels despite similar costs for the products themselves.
There are separate weekly data available from the European Commission about fuel prices before and after tax inclusion, which enables the role of taxes in the matter to be evaluated.
Taxes on gasoline and diesel are also imposed in the United States at both the federal and state levels. Still, there is a difference between the tax burden and pricing policy in the country and some European states.
Another aspect here is the different energy policies of the two continents. In Europe, fuel taxation has been traditionally used as a tool for managing consumption and generating income.
Lower taxes on fuel in the US have enabled the nation to maintain lower prices of fuel compared to those of Europe.
However, domestic crude production and the nation’s refinery and distribution capability have had an impact on the market, while crude prices are still influenced by international trends.
It would be erroneous to claim that the entire price differential can be attributed to a single cause. It is due to taxes, refining costs, distribution costs, and exchange rates, among others.
 Will the gap between US and EU gas prices continue?
While the difference in prices may continue, it is by no means certain to maintain its present value.
International crude oil prices will continue to be relevant factors influencing pricing in both countries. Events involving global oil supplies, geopolitics, production, and refining can make petrol and diesel prices move up or down in either direction.
Recent US data also point out that fuel prices have been facing pressure.
According to a report by the American Automobile Association earlier this week, the national average price for gasoline stood at $4.10 per gallon, which represents a decrease of 12 cents from the previous week but is still about $1 higher than a year ago.
Europe is exposed to the same effects of international energy market developments, but due to the high fuel tax rate in Europe, changes in international crude oil prices may not be immediately reflected in petrol and diesel prices.
Also, there is the factor of currency valuation. An appreciation of the dollar over the euro could cause the price of gasoline in the United States to look more expensive once the price is converted into euros, despite no change in the US price.
What this means for consumers is that the cost of fuel goes beyond just the price of crude oil.
The tax rates of the government, energy policies within the country and other market forces in the domestic environment could mean that the prices of gasoline in two countries that have equal access to global crude oil are vastly different.
In conclusion, Americans benefit from a clear price advantage over people from the EU, especially when buying petrol.
